title: Architectures for engineering data: MLP, CNN, and sequence models

items.context:
An 8 by 8 temperature field goes through one 3 by 3 convolution with no
padding, giving a 6 by 6 feature map. A colleague proposes a dense layer
from the same 64 inputs to the same 36 outputs instead, since "it can learn
anything the convolution can."

How many weights does each need, and why does the difference matter for a
stress or temperature field?
items.why:
Parameter sharing: one set of nine weights slides over every position, so an
edge detector learned in one corner works in all of them. The dense layer
has 64 x 36 = 2,304 weights and has to learn each position's detector
separately, from far more data. The dense layer can represent the
convolution, but it would need the data to discover a symmetry the
convolution builds in.
items.true: 9 for the convolution against 2,304 for the dense layer, because the same kernel is reused at every position
false: Both need 2,304, because every output must still see every input; the convolution only reorders the arithmetic
36 for the convolution, one per output position, against 2,304, because each position learns its own kernel
9 against 64, since a dense layer needs one weight per input and a convolution one per kernel cell

items.context:
A 1D-CNN reads 30-cycle sensor windows through three stacked convolution
layers, each with a width-5 kernel and "same" padding, stride 1, no
dilation.

How many cycles of the window can influence one output of the third layer?
items.why:
Each layer adds k - 1 = 4 cycles of reach, so three layers give
1 + 3 x 4 = 13, less than half the window. Padding keeps the output length
but adds no reach; near the window's edge some of those 13 inputs are
padding zeros. Dilating the layers by 1, 2 and 4 widens the reach to 29
cycles with the same number of weights.
items.true: 13 cycles, because each layer adds 4 cycles beyond the first
false: 5 cycles, because stacking layers does not widen what one kernel sees
15 cycles, because each layer adds its full kernel width of 5
30 cycles, because same padding lets every output see the whole window

items.context:
A plain RNN on 30-cycle windows learns almost nothing from the early cycles
of each window. A teammate's fix is to add
`torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)` to the training
loop and retrain.

What is wrong with the fix?
items.why:
Backpropagation through the recurrence multiplies by roughly the same factor
at each step, so the signal reaching cycle 1 is that factor to the 29th
power. Below 1 it vanishes, and clipping only ever shrinks a gradient. The
GRU's state path multiplies by (1 - z), which training can hold near 1, so
the gradient can pass through many steps intact.
items.true: Clipping only shrinks large gradients; the early cycles get vanishing ones, which a gated cell such as a GRU fixes
false: The threshold is too high; clipping at 0.1 instead would rescale the early-cycle gradients up to a size the optimizer can actually use
Clipping belongs after `optimizer.step()`, so as written it runs too late to affect the update
Nothing; clipping is the standard remedy for recurrent networks and is enough on its own

items.context:
A GRU trained on FD001 windows scores about 14 cycles of RUL RMSE on
held-out engines. You score it again on the same windows with the 30
cycles reversed in time.

Before you look: what happens to its error?
items.why:
The GRU scored 13.91 recorded and 59.32 reversed, averaged over five
engine-grouped folds. Its state has only ever seen degradation run forward,
so a reversed window looks like an engine getting healthier. The recurrent
prior assumes the input is a trajectory, and on this data the assumption is
correct, which is why the GRU scores well recorded and collapses reversed.
items.true: Past 59 cycles, worse than predicting the training mean for every window
false: Roughly unchanged, since the GRU sees exactly the same 30 readings either way
A cycle or two worse, about what the positional transformer loses
Slightly better, since reversal puts the most degraded readings first

items.context:
Four models on FD001 30-cycle windows, scored by RUL RMSE over five
engine-grouped folds and five seeds:

**A.** gradient-boosted trees on window summaries
**B.** a GRU
**C.** a transformer with a learned positional encoding
**D.** a 1D-CNN

Rank them best (lowest RMSE) first.
items.why:
Boosted trees 13.29, GRU 14.03, transformer 16.39, 1D-CNN 17.77. The
transformer trails the GRU because it assumes the least: order has to be
learned from a position table and any cycle may matter to any other, and
about 70 training engines per fold is little data to learn that from. Its
best validation epoch is typically the sixth, against the GRU's sixteenth.
items.true: A, then B, then C, then D
false: C, then B, then D, then A
B, then C, then A, then D
D, then B, then A, then C

items.context:
You read the attention weights out of the trained FD001 transformer. In the
first layer every row's entropy is at least 99% of the maximum, and the model
averages its outputs over the 30 cycles before the prediction head.

What is the model computing, to a first approximation?
items.why:
Near-uniform weights make each output close to the window mean of the
values, and the mean over cycles afterwards keeps it there. The second layer
is slightly sharper, putting 28% of the last row on the last five cycles
against 17% uniform. Head-averaging can hide a sharper head, so this is a
statement about the average; it still means a story about "the model
attends to the failure precursor" needs checking before anyone tells it.
items.true: Something close to a nonlinear function of window averages, the summaries boosting already gets
false: A sharp lookup of the few cycles nearest failure, which the linear head then extrapolates to a RUL
Nothing useful; uniform attention means the layers never trained
A learned recurrence, since stacked attention layers recover sequential order on their own

items.context:
"Transformers are state of the art for long-horizon time-series
forecasting." Someone cites the Informer and Autoformer line of work.

What did Zeng and colleagues (AAAI 2023) report when they revisited those
benchmarks?
items.why:
LTSF-Linear "surprisingly outperforms existing sophisticated
Transformer-based LTSF models in all cases, and often by a large margin."
Two explanations: self-attention is permutation-invariant and loses
temporal information, and the earlier baselines forecast iteratively while
the transformers predicted the whole horizon at once, so a direct linear
model was missing from the comparison.
items.true: That one-layer linear models beat every transformer on nine datasets, often by a large margin
false: That the transformers still won, but only on the longest forecast horizons and the largest datasets
That the transformers and linear models tied once all of them were tuned equally
That the benchmark datasets leaked the forecast horizon into the input window

items.context:
A GRU is trained with Adam, early stopping at patience 10, and
`CosineAnnealingLR(opt, T_max=60)` for a 60-epoch budget. The kept epoch
lands between 9 and 17. You rerun with a constant learning rate and nothing
else changed.

What happens to the best validation RMSE?
items.why:
13.04 against 13.04, and four of five seeds stopped on the same epoch under
both schedules. At epoch 17 the cosine rate is still 83% of its starting
value, so the schedule does most of its decaying during epochs early
stopping throws away. Pairing a schedule with early stopping means checking
the learning rate at the epoch you actually keep.
items.true: It is unchanged to two decimals, because the cosine rate had barely decayed by the epochs early stopping kept
false: It rises clearly, because the decaying cosine rate is what let the GRU settle into the bottom of the minimum
It falls clearly, because a constant rate keeps exploring after cosine would have frozen
It becomes erratic across seeds, because a constant rate never reduces the minibatch noise near the minimum

items.context:
Early stopping is usually described as a way to save compute. Goodfellow,
Bengio and Courville (section 7.8) show it is also a regularizer.

For a linear model with quadratic loss trained by gradient descent from
small weights, what is it equivalent to?
items.why:
Starting from small weights, gradient descent moves them outward over time,
so stopping after fewer steps keeps them smaller, much as a stronger L2
penalty would. Training longer is like regularizing less. The same book's
Algorithm 7.1 is the patience rule the lecture uses.
items.true: L2 regularization, with the number of steps playing the role of the reciprocal of the penalty
false: Dropout, with the number of steps setting the drop probability
Gradient clipping, since both cap how far the weights can move
A learning-rate schedule, since stopping amounts to setting the rate to zero from that step onward

items.context:
The lecture's GRU clips gradients at norm 1.0 and logs the pre-clip norm.
After the first epoch the median batch norm is about 0.12, and the largest
batch in any epoch never exceeds 0.54.

What is clipping doing in this run?
items.why:
Only the first epoch had batches above 1.0, about a quarter of them. Clipping
rescales a gradient only when its norm exceeds the threshold, so it is
insurance here. Setting the threshold at the median norm would clip half of
all steps and act as a second learning rate. `clip_grad_norm_` returns the
pre-clip norm, so logging whether the threshold is ever reached costs
nothing.
items.true: Acting only during the first epoch, while the weights are random, and doing nothing afterwards
false: Acting on every batch, which is why the GRU trains stably at all
Slowing training throughout, since any threshold shrinks every step a little
Nothing measurable here, but the logged norms show the threshold should be lowered to about 0.12

items.context:
A two-weight loss pins one weight down firmly (high curvature) and the
other only loosely (low curvature). Without a penalty the optimum is
(2.40, 1.60). You add weight decay.

How does the penalty move the two weights?
items.why:
With lambda = 0.5 the optimum moves to (2.06, 0.53): the firm weight keeps
86% and the loose one 33%. Weight decay rescales the optimum along each
Hessian eigenvector by lambda_i / (lambda_i + alpha), so it removes the parts
of the fit the data barely supports, which are the parts most likely to be
fitting noise.
items.true: The loose weight shrinks far more: it keeps about a third, the firm one most of its value
false: Both shrink by the same fraction, since the penalty coefficient is the same for every weight
The firm weight shrinks more, since the larger weight carries the larger squared penalty
Neither moves, since weight decay only changes the path, not the optimum

items.context:
Open [`l12-cnn-rul.ipynb`](../lectures/l12/l12-cnn-rul.ipynb), run it top
to bottom, and look at the order test in section 6, which scores each
network on its windows recorded, reversed, and shuffled.

Which pattern should you see, whatever your exact numbers?
items.why:
Without a positional encoding, attention followed by a mean over cycles
treats the window as a set, so reversing or shuffling it changes nothing, to
the last digit. The positional transformer uses order but leans on it
lightly; the GRU, whose computation is a walk along the cycles, is hurt
most. The notes' five-fold version of the table shows the same pattern:
17.87 on every view without positions, against 13.91 recorded and 59.32
reversed for the GRU.
items.true: The transformer without positions scores the same on all three views, and the GRU degrades most
false: Every network gets somewhat worse on reversed windows, and by roughly the same amount
The positional transformer degrades most, since attention compares every pair of cycles and is the most order-sensitive
No network changes, since each one averages over the window before predicting
